hints: Look at the carbon joined to two oxygens in ibuprofen on the right side, one as C=O and one as OH. What combined group does this make?
Look at paracetamol carefully, there is an OH joined directly to the benzene ring and a nitrogen joined to a C=O. Recall how these two groups are named when attached in these ways.
walkthrough:
Read the ibuprofen side chain**
Focus on the right hand end of ibuprofen, $\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-C(=O)-OH}$. A carbon with both a C=O and an OH on the same carbon is the classic $\text{-COOH}$ group. That is a carboxylic acid.

Read the two oxygen and nitrogen groups in paracetamol**
On the right, $\text{-OH}$ is joined directly to the benzene ring. An OH joined directly to an aryl ring is a phenol, not an alcohol. On the left, $\text{CH}_3\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ has nitrogen joined to a carbonyl carbon. That $\text{-CONH-}$ link is an amide.

Final answer: ibuprofen: carboxylic acid (carboxyl group)
paracetamol: phenol and amide

hints: Think about what makes a carbon asymmetric, how many groups must it hold and how must they compare to each other?
walkthrough:
Picture the tetrahedral carbon**
Imagine a carbon with four single bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. If all four attached groups are different, there is no plane of symmetry and the mirror image cannot be superimposed. That carbon is a chiral centre.
Final answer: A chiral centre is a carbon (atom) bonded to four different atoms or groups.

hints: Find the carbon in ibuprofen joined to the ring, to H, to $\text{CH}_3$ and to $\text{COOH}$. That is the only carbon with four different groups.
Recall that the two enantiomers are mirror images, so draw the same four groups but swap the 3D positions of two groups using solid wedge and hashed wedge bonds.
walkthrough:
Locate the chiral carbon**
In ibuprofen the carbon next to the ring is bonded to: the aryl ring, $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$, and $\text{COOH}$. Those four are all different, so this is the stereocentre. No other carbon qualifies.

Draw a mirror image pair**
Keep the skeleton the same but show 3D clearly. Draw the central C with four bonds: one to Ar, one to $\text{COOH}$, one wedge to $\text{CH}_3$ and one dash to H for one enantiomer. For the second enantiomer, reverse the wedge and dash exactly. The two structures must be mirror images that cannot be superimposed.

Final answer: Two non-superimposable mirror images centred on $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)(COOH)}$.
One isomer has e.g. $\text{CH}_3$ on wedge and H on dash, the other has $\text{CH}_3$ on dash and H on wedge, with $\text{Ar}$ and $\text{COOH}$ in the plane.

hints: Remember $\text{LiAlH}_4$ is a strong reducing agent that reduces $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and reduces amides to amines, but leaves benzene rings and phenols unchanged in terms of carbon skeleton.
For paracetamol focus on the $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH-}$ part, the C=O oxygen is removed and two hydrogens are added to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH-}$.
walkthrough:
Reduce the acid in ibuprofen**
$\text{LiAlH}_4$ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon. A carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$ is reduced all the way to a primary alcohol $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$. So $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)-COOH}$ becomes $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{OH}$. The benzene ring is untouched.

Reduce the amide in paracetamol**
Paracetamol contains a secondary amide $\text{CH}_3\text{-C(=O)-NH-Ar}$. $\text{LiAlH}_4$ removes the carbonyl oxygen and adds hydrogen, giving a secondary amine $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-NH-Ar}$. The phenol $\text{Ar-OH}$ stays as $\text{Ar-OH}$ in the organic skeleton, so the product is 4-(ethylamino)phenol.

Final answer: product with ibuprofen: $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{OH}$, i.e. $\text{COOH}$ reduced to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.
product with paracetamol: $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, i.e. $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH-}$ reduced to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH-}$, phenolic $\text{OH}$ retained.

hints: Reagent D reacts only with ibuprofen which has a $\text{COOH}$ group. Think which weak base reacts with a carboxylic acid with effervescence but is not strong enough to react appreciably with a phenol or amide under these test conditions.

Reagent E reacts only with paracetamol which has an activated phenol ring. Think which reagent gives a rapid white precipitate or decolourisation with phenols by substitution at positions ortho to the OH.
walkthrough:
Link D to the carboxylic acid**
Only ibuprofen reacts with D. Ibuprofen has $\text{-COOH}$, a stronger acid than phenol. Carbonate, for example $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, will deprotonate a carboxylic acid to give $\text{CO}_2$ effervescence, but phenol in paracetamol is too weak an acid to react in the same way. So D is a carbonate.

Link E to the phenol**
Only paracetamol reacts with E. The phenol ring is strongly activated toward electrophilic substitution. Bromine water, $\text{Br}_2$, or chlorine, $\text{Cl}_2$, rapidly substitutes ortho to the $\text{OH}$ group. Ibuprofen has only an alkylbenzene ring which does not react under these mild conditions without a catalyst.

Final answer: D: $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ or $\text{NaHCO}_3$ or any carbonate / hydrogencarbonate
E: $\text{Br}_2$ (bromine water) or $\text{Cl}_2$

hints: Think what happens to $\text{-COOH}$ when it reacts with carbonate, which proton is lost and what sodium containing group replaces it?
walkthrough:
Convert the acid to its salt**
The $\text{COOH}$ proton is removed by carbonate to give $\text{COO}^-$. With sodium present the organic product is $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)-COONa}$. Draw the full ibuprofen skeleton unchanged except $\text{COOH}$ becomes $\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$.
Final answer: Sodium salt of ibuprofen: $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_3\text{)-COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ ( $\text{COONa}$ group, rest of molecule unchanged).

hints: Recall that the OH group strongly activates ortho and para positions, but in paracetamol the para position is already blocked by the amide group, so consider where two bromine atoms will enter.
walkthrough:
Place two bromines ortho to the phenol**
The $\text{OH}$ group directs incoming electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions. Position 4 is occupied by $\text{NHCOCH}_3$, so substitution occurs twice, at both ortho positions. Draw paracetamol with Br at the two carbons next to the $\text{OH}$, keeping $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NHCOCH}_3$ intact.
Final answer: 2,6-dibromo-paracetamol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH-C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_2\text{-OH}$ with Br atoms ortho to $\text{OH}$ on both sides, amide and phenol groups retained.

hints: Think how the Lewis acid $\text{AlCl}_3$ pulls $\text{Cl}^-$ away from $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ to leave a positively charged carbon electrophile and a chloroaluminate anion.
walkthrough:
Generate the acylium ion**
$\text{AlCl}_3$ is an electron pair acceptor. It takes $\text{Cl}^-$ from ethanoyl chloride, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$. That leaves the acylium ion $\text{CH}_3\text{C} \equiv \text{O}^+$, usually written $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$, plus $\text{AlCl}_4^-$. This $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ is the strong electrophile for the next step.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+ + \text{AlCl}_4^-$

hints: Start with the benzene pi electrons in X attacking the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ electrophile, draw a curly arrow from the ring to the carbonyl carbon.
Think what the ring looks like after attack, a positively charged cyclohexadienyl intermediate with the $\text{COCH}_3$ group now attached and the positive charge delocalised in the ring.
Consider how aromaticity is restored, which bond breaks to reform the pi system and where does its pair of electrons go, and what happens to the ring H at the site of attack?
walkthrough:
Attack the electrophile with the ring**
The benzene pi cloud in X is electron rich. Draw a curly arrow starting in the centre of the ring (or from a C=C bond) and pointing to the carbon atom of $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$. This forms a new $\text{C-C}$ bond between the ring and the $\text{COCH}_3$ group.

Show the positively charged intermediate**
Attack breaks the aromaticity. Draw the cyclohexadienyl cation (Wheland intermediate) with the $\text{COCH}_3$ group and the original H both attached to the same tetrahedral carbon, and the positive charge delocalised over the other ring carbons. This is the key high energy intermediate.

Remove the proton to regain the benzene ring**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond at the substitution site back into the ring to reform the pi system. The H leaves as $\text{H}^+$ (later picked up by $\text{AlCl}_4^-$). The ring becomes aromatic again, giving the para-acyl product Y.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system of X to C of $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ to form $\text{C-C}$ bond and arenium ion with $\text{COCH}_3$ attached and positive charge in ring.
Correct Wheland intermediate with H still attached at substitution site.
Curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond back into ring to restore aromaticity, losing $\text{H}^+$ to give Y.

hints: Recall the general class where an electrophile replaces a hydrogen on a benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Name the pattern**
A positive electrophile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$, attacks the benzene ring and replaces H. Attack by an electrophile followed by substitution that restores aromaticity is electrophilic substitution, here a Friedel-Crafts acylation.
Final answer: electrophilic substitution (electrophilic aromatic substitution / Friedel-Crafts acylation)
